readerTitle: The manager who thought her door was always open
caseNote: 가상 사례 (철물점 매니저, 마케팅 컨설팅사) + 실제 연구 (Tasha Eurich의 자기 인식 연구)
insight: 자기 인식은 내 의도를 아는 것이 아니라, 내 행동 패턴과 그것이 남에게 어떻게 닿는지를 아는 것이다. 이는 '왜'가 아니라 '무엇' 질문으로 보인다.
misconception: 나는 내 의도를 잘 아니까 나를 잘 안다. 자기 인식은 혼자 깊이 생각하면 생긴다.

sources.text: Eurich, T. (2018). What Self-Awareness Really Is (and How to Cultivate It). Harvard Business Review.
철물점과 컨설팅사 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: "약 95%가 자신이 자기 인식이 있다고 믿지만 실제로는 10~15%뿐"이라는 수치는 Eurich(2018, HBR)의 추정입니다. 원문 표현과 수치 범위를 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요.
내적 자기 인식과 외적 자기 인식의 상관이 낮다는 결과, '왜(why)'보다 '무엇(what)' 질문이 통찰에 더 도움이 된다는 결과가 Eurich의 연구 보고에 있는지 확인하세요.
"경험과 권력이 자기 평가의 정확도가 아니라 자신감을 높인다"는 내용이 Eurich(2018)에 나오는지 확인하세요. 카드에는 "suggests"로 완화해 적었습니다.
"연구팀이 수천 명을 연구했다"는 표현이 원문과 맞는지 확인하세요. 정확한 표본 수는 일부러 적지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The manager who thought her door was always open
body: Dana runs a busy hardware store. She often tells her team they can bring her any problem, any time.
At the Monday meeting she asks what's going wrong. Nobody says a word. Yet the store tells another story: wrong stock on the shelves, a missed delivery, a broken scanner nobody reported.

image.label: A store manager facing a silent team in an aisle
image.brief: 철물점 통로에서 매니저가 직원 네 명 앞에 서서 질문하는 장면. 직원들은 시선을 피하고 말이 없다. 배경 선반에는 잘못 놓인 상품, 계산대 위에 고장 난 스캐너. 따뜻한 일러스트 톤. 실제 매장 브랜드나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Why is the team so quiet?
body: Dana believes she's approachable. But her staff clearly aren't bringing her problems.

options.text: Remind everyone, clearly, that her door is always open
options.feedback: It repeats her intention, not their experience. If something she does makes people go quiet, a reminder changes nothing.

options.text: Watch what she herself does in the moments when problems come up
options.feedback: It costs some pride, but it looks for the one cause she fully controls. That's the idea in this lesson.
Useful, and a later lesson covers it. But the answers will make more sense once she has noticed her own reactions.

cards.title: Dana kept notes for one week.
body: Each time someone brought her a problem, she wrote one line: what was happening, what she said, how she felt.
The pattern was plain. During the morning delivery rush, she cut people off mid-sentence, asked who was responsible and took over the fix. She thought she was being helpful. Her staff heard blame.
They didn't stop having problems. They stopped bringing them to her.

cards.title: Self-awareness
body: **Self-awareness** is seeing yourself clearly: your own habits and reactions, and how they land on other people.

It has two sides. *Inner* self-awareness is knowing what you value and what sets you off. *Outer* self-awareness is knowing how others experience you. Dana knew her intention well. She didn't know her impact.

image.label: Two sides: what I intend vs how others see me
image.brief: 좌우 분할 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "Inner: what I value, what sets me off" (사람 머릿속 아이콘), 오른쪽 "Outer: how others experience me" (주변 사람들의 시선 아이콘). 가운데에 "Intent ≠ Impact" 문구. 깔끔한 플랫 스타일.

cards.title: Most of us overrate ourselves.
body: Organizational psychologist Tasha Eurich and her team studied thousands of people. She estimates that about 95% believe they are self-aware, but only 10–15% really are.

Two more findings stand out. The inner and outer sides aren't closely linked, so knowing your values doesn't mean you know how you come across. And people who asked *what* questions, such as "What situations set me off?", gained more insight than those who asked *why*.

cards.title: Patterns hide in plain sight.
body: Every workplace has its version of Dana's morning rush:
list: A chef who goes silent under pressure, so cooks stop asking questions at the worst moment
A warehouse supervisor who praises in private but criticizes in public
A shop owner who calms angry customers well but doesn't know it, so never teaches it
cards.callout: Self-awareness covers strengths too. A habit you can't see, you can't share.
cards.softwareNote: A founder who rewrites engineers' code late at night may think she's helping. The team may read it as "my work is never good enough" and stop shipping without her review.

cards.title: Looking inward has limits.
body: Thinking harder about yourself can turn into rumination: endless "why am I like this?" loops that bring stress, not insight.
And you can't fully see the outer side alone. Your notes show what you did. Only other people can tell you how it felt.
Eurich's work also suggests that experience and power tend to make people more confident in their self-view, not more accurate. The higher you rise, the less people tell you.

image.label: A person stuck in a loop of thought bubbles
image.brief: 한 사람이 책상에 앉아 머리 위에 "Why?" 말풍선이 원을 그리며 반복되는 장면. 옆에는 작은 창문 너머로 동료들이 보이는데, 이 사람은 그쪽을 보지 않는다. 차분한 색감.

cards.title: Now it's a consulting firm.
body: You lead client projects at a small marketing consultancy. Two clients left this year. Both said, politely, that they "didn't feel heard."
You think of yourself as a good listener. What's your first move?

options.text: Spend an evening reflecting on why you don't listen
options.feedback: Reflection is a fair start, but *why* questions tend to produce stories and self-blame rather than patterns you can change.

options.text: After your next three client calls, note what you did: how long you talked, when you jumped to solutions
options.feedback: It's uncomfortable, but it turns a vague complaint into specific behavior you can see and change.

options.text: Decide those two clients simply weren't a good fit
options.feedback: It protects your self-image, but it keeps a habit that may cost you the next client too.

cards.title: Your intentions are not your impact.
body: Self-awareness means knowing both what you do and how it lands. Look for your patterns with *what* questions, not *why*.
**Try it today:** pick one tense moment that keeps recurring at work. Next time it happens, write one line afterward: what happened, what you did, what happened next.
